segments.text: What is up developers? Welcome back to GitHub awesome. Today we're looking at 35 self-hosted projects on GitHub. Let's get into it.
Tudoist and Things are polished tools that store your entire life on someone else's servers and charge monthly for the privilege. Tudy is the self-hosted
alternative built around a different philosophy entirely. Tasks, projects, notes, and areas with smart workflows tying them together running on your own
server. No gamified streaks, no notification badges, no anxietyinducing UI, just a quiet place to think and plan.
Setting up a self-hosted wiki shouldn't mean inheriting another complex production stack to monitor. Leaf wiki is built specifically to keep your engineering docs simple and independent.
It packages a clean web interface as a single Go binary with zero external database dependencies. It stores all
your content directly on disk as plain markdown files, making backups as easy as a standard folder copy.
Many developers build their best side projects simply because the commercial alternatives are way too expensive or
packed with useless features. Lingua Cafe is a self-hosted language learning platform born from that exact frustration. It lets you import ebooks
and YouTube subtitles to read in your target language. The app automatically parses words and schedules spaced
repetition reviews, keeping your study logs fully local.
If you love Google's Notebook LM, but hate sending private research papers straight to big tech servers, you need to check out Open Notebook. It is a
self-hosted alternative that runs on your own hardware using Docker. You can ingest PDFs or web pages, then chat with
your data using local models through Olama. It gives you a complete REST API and even generates custom podcasts with up to four speakers.
Obsidian and notion keep piling on features until notetaking feels like a second job. Many notes goes the other direction on purpose. It's a markdown
note-taking web app designed around one idea, simplicity. Organize your notes in vaults. Write in plain markdown. And
that's largely the point. No plug-in marketplace to manage. No database lockin, just clean, fast notes you self-host and own.
Obsidian on a borrowed laptop means remote desktop or paying for their sync service. Ignis runs Obsidian as a genuine self-hosted web app, not screen
streaming, an actual web app you open in a browser. Your full Obsidian setup, plugins and all, running on your own server, accessible from any browser
anywhere. Your notes, your plugins, your infrastructure. No Obsidian Sync subscription required.
Sometimes you don't want a knowledge base with backlinks and graph views. You just want a blank page to dump a thought right now. Scratch is built for exactly
that. It's a minimalist offline first markdown note app. Open it and you're already typing. No account, no setup, no
sync nagging you. Offline first means it works instantly with no connection and your notes live on your device.
SAS platforms that charge you perm minute fees and store your private meeting recordings in their cloud are a total racket. Speaker is a self-hosted
alternative that turns your audio files into a searchable private knowledge base. It handles speaker diorization and
semantic search entirely on your own hardware. You can record live audio and stack custom AI summary prompts with zero data leaks.
Stop feeding your private files to sketchy online converters just to crop an image or parse some JSON. Omni Tools
lets you self-host your own browserbased toolbox using a tiny 28 megabyte Docker image. Because everything executes
client side on your own machine, you get complete data privacy with zero tracking. It covers dozens of everyday utilities from video cropping to hex encoding completely offline.
Run a home lab and your services live at a dozen random IP and port combos you can never remember. Homer puts them all
on one page. It's a modern, easy to use dashboard that ties your whole setup together. Over 40 integrations that pull
live status from the apps you run, 20,000 plus icons built in and authentication out of the box. The best
part for anyone who's fought Heimdoll or Dashy, no YAML.
Where's the model number on your furnace? When was the water heater installed? Which paint color is in the hallway? That information lives in a
drawer of manuals in your memory until you need it. Home information organizes all of it. It's a self-hosted app built
around a visual map of your home. You place your equipment, appliances, and systems on it, then attach manuals,
maintenance history, warranties, and notes to each one. Paying a monthly subscription just to sync your SSH keys
and server bookmarks across devices is a massive tax on your home lab. Termix gives you a completely free self-hosted
alternative to Termius. You run the server in Docker and it syncs your connection profiles and active tunnels across all your screens. It even
features a built-in SFTP file editor and a basic container manager right in your browser.
Your AI coding agent treats every file as equally important and has no idea your codebase has a 4,000line module
nobody's touched in two years. Repo wise gives it the lay of the land. It's a codebase intelligence layer for AI
assisted teams. Code health scores, autogenerated docs, git analytics, dead code detection, and a record of
architectural decisions all exposed to your agent over MCP.
You've got a beefy GPU in your gaming rig and a CPUon home server that desperately wants it for AI workloads.
Normally, that GPU is trapped in one box.
Lupine breaks it loose. It's a GPU over IP bridge that attaches a GPU on a remote machine to a CPUon machine over
your network so your server can run inference or training on a graphics card that physically lives somewhere else in the house.
Firebase locks you in. Superbase self-hosted means running Postgress plus a stack of services. Trailbase strips it
down to a single executable. Types safe APIs, real-time subscriptions, O and an admin UI, all built on Rust and SQLite,
a built-in web assembly runtime via Womtime lets you write custom server logic in any language that compiles to WASM. A complete Firebase alternative in one file.
Running a home server means choosing between wasting electricity 24/7 or manually managing sleep and wake cycles.
Dsomnia is a declarative network aware sleep manager that handles it automatically. It monitors active user
sessions and open SMB shares, sends the host to sleep once everything goes quiet, then intercepts incoming
connections and transparently wakes the server on demand.
Most HomeLab dashboards require editing a config file and restarting every time you add a service. Dinoat skips that
entirely. Change your layout, add a service, and it updates live with no restart and no downtime. Built around
dynamic reloading from the start with clean integration hooks so your self-hosted tools show real status without friction. A dashboard that stays
out of your way while your home lab evolves.
Everyone backs up their Postgress database. Almost nobody verifies those backups restore correctly until the moment they desperately need one.
Databases handles both halves. Point in time recovery lets you roll back to any exact moment before a bad migration or
an accidental delete. The restore verification actually tests that your backups work instead of assuming they do.
Run a real stack and you've probably got Postgress, a Reddus cache, maybe MongoDB and a MySQL service from that one legacy
app. And backing each one up means a different tool and a different cron job.
Porterbase unifies it. It's a single backup and restore tool that speaks Poster SQL, MySQL, Mariab, Firebird,
SQLite, MongoDB, Reddus, and Valky with more engines on the way.
Open Table charges per cover fees, owns your customer data, and puts their brand between you and your diners. Open Resto
is a self-hosted booking system with no fees, no data collection, and no ads.
Run multiple restaurants from one instance. Communicate with customers from your own email address and give diners a clean, mobile friendly booking
UI that isn't pushing them toward competitor restaurants.
Strava locks the interesting analytics behind a subscription and even then you're seeing your data their way.
Statistics for Strava pulls your full activity history into a self-hosted dashboard you control. Rich charts,
detailed breakdowns, no premium tier, no payw wall on data you already generated.
Your training history on your own server analyzed however you want. Your miles, your insights, no subscription required.
Self-hosted notes apps often feel sluggish, loading spinners, laggy editors, sync that stalls. Notemark's
entire pitch is speed. It's a lightning fast web-based markdown notes app. Open it and the editor is instantly responsive. Your notes stored as plain
markdown you own served from your own machine. No bloat, no plug-in sprawl, just a quick place to write and organize.
You SSH into your Raspberry Pi and run htop, but it tells you nothing about temperature, throttling, or whether that
flaky power supply is browning out under load. System PI gives you the full picture. It's a modern real-time
monitoring dashboard for the Pi. Live telemetry on CPU, memory, and network, plus hardware health diagnostics like
temperature and throttle state, the things that actually kill a PI project.
Kokuro is the tiny 82 million parameter TTS model everyone loves for sounding shockingly natural at its size, but running it means wrangling Python and
model weights yourself. Kokoro fast API makes it a service. It's a dockerized fast API wrapper that exposes Kokoro
behind a clean API with CPU support via ONX and NVIDIA GPU acceleration via PyTorch, plus autostitching so long text flows into one seamless audio file.
A journaling habit means trusting your most private thoughts to an app. And most of them are someone's cloud subscription that can change terms, get
breached, or shut down. Jouv is a self-hosted private journaling app.
Write your daily entries on your own server, your reflections, your memories, your bad days, all staying on hardware
you control instead of a company's database.
GitHub actions is easy until your bill balloons. and self-hosted Jenkins is a sprawling mess of plugins and a server you babysit. PicoCI aims for the middle.
It's a CI/CD system that ships as one binary and works with any database and any queue. So you start tiny and scale
the same tool up as your needs grow. No replatforming. Runs anywhere on your laptop, a VPS or a real cluster.
You want an RSS reader, but you don't want to run a server or trust a hosted app with your reading list. Liveboat does an end run around both. It's a
template that builds your own personalized RSS feed site and publishes it on GitHub pages. Free hosting, no
server to maintain. A GitHub action fetches your feeds on a schedule and regenerates a clean static site you read from anywhere.
Mint is dead. WAB wants a yearly subscription and both want to link directly to your bank. Budget Board
keeps it simple and yours. It's a self-hosted app for tracking your monthly spending and working toward financial goals. Log where your money
goes, watch your categories, and measure progress against the targets you set, all on your own server. No subscription,
no third party reading your transactions.
Most commercial fitness apps make money by locking your health logs behind a payw wall and selling your data. Sparky Fitness fixes this by letting you spin
up a private multi-user health tracker using Docker. It is a self-hosted alternative to My Fitness Pal built
natively for families. It syncs steps and workouts from Apple Health and even logs meals automatically through plain text or photo uploads.
Wrestling with complex federated protocols or bloated instant messaging servers just to host a private chat room for your friends is a massive headache.
Sunburn tackles this by packaging your real time text and media feeds into a streamlined self-hosted stack built
entirely on Pocket Base and Live Kit. It runs inside a single lightweight backend container.
An unplanned power outage doesn't just cut your lights. It's a fast way to corrupt your unmounted local file systems. Eneroo fixes this by acting as
a smart shutdown orchestrator for network UPS tools. Instead of cutting power immediately, it monitors your UPS
battery and safely shuts down your virtual machines or docker containers in a strict orderly sequence. It even features an embedded browser dashboard and Prometheus metrics out of the box.
Running your own mail server means raw IMAP unless you add a web mail client on top. RoundCube has been that client for
over a decade. A clean Gmail style browser interface for any IMAP server with folders, search, address book, and
a plug-in system for extensions. Battle tested at massive scale. It's the web mail client that ships with cPanel and countless hosting providers.
Mobile crash reporting usually means a heavy third party SDK bloating your binary and shipping user data to someone
else's cloud. Red is a lightweight self-hosted alternative. Open- source observability for mobile apps built to
stay performant. So you get crash data, errors, and usage insights without the SDK overhead or user data leaving your control.
Landing a highly competitive apartment lease in Germany usually means staring at listing feeds all day just to be the first applicant. Freddy automates this
search by running a self-hosted scraper across multiple real estate portals. It reverse engineers mobile APIs to fetch
listings. the second they go live, instantly delivering updates to Telegram or Discord.
MTLS is one of the best ways to lock down self-hosted services, and manually managing certificates with OpenSSL commands is genuinely miserable.
VaultTLS makes it manageable. A self-hosted web app that handles your entire mutual TLS setup. Create your certificate authority, issue client
certificates through a clean UI, distribute them without touching the command line.
[music]
